issues.legal_issue: Taking recourse to an available statutory remedy to address a company-management deadlock, and acting under interim directions made in that proceeding, does not by itself establish civil contempt where wilful disobedience of a court order or undertaking is not proved.
material_facts: The respondents approached the company-law forum alleging that disagreement among the directors had stalled the company’s operations and harmed the company and its employees.
The company-law forum appointed a facilitator to address urgent operational matters and later expanded the facilitator’s role in resolving disagreements between directors.

The Supreme Court’s subsequent orders acknowledged the facilitator’s role, stated that its own arrangements would not interfere with that role, and continued the existing arrangement for running the company.

The petitioner did not obtain an order setting aside the company-law forum’s directions, and the contempt petition alleged that resort to that forum and the resulting directions breached the earlier settlement orders.
The Court found that the petitioner had not established wilful, deliberate, and intentional disobedience of a direction or breach of an undertaking given to the Court.
issues.conclusion: The contempt petition was dismissed because the petitioner failed to establish civil contempt; the respondents’ resort to the available legal remedy and the orders made in that proceeding did not, on these facts, amount to wilful disobedience.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(b) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 requires wilful disobedience of a court order or wilful breach of an undertaking. Contempt proceedings are quasi-criminal, require a clear case of deliberate disobedience, and are not execution proceedings. The Court relied on Niaz Mohammad v. State of Haryana, Kanwar Singh Saini v. High Court of Delhi, and Debabrata Bandopadhyaya v. State of West Bengal on the requirement of intentional disobedience and the benefit of doubt; Pratap Singh v. Gurbaksh Singh and Mehar Rusi Dalal v. T.K. Banerjee on the right to pursue legal remedies; and Sections 397, 398, and 403 of the Companies Act, 1956, which authorized company-law proceedings and interim orders to regulate company affairs.

rule.if: civil_contempt_proceeding and respondent_used_available_legal_remedy and remedy_addressed_company_management_deadlock and interim_facilitator_arrangement_recognized_by_court and interim_orders_not_set_aside and not wilful_disobedience

predicates.civil_contempt_proceeding: The matter is a proceeding seeking a finding of civil contempt for disobedience of a court order or breach of an undertaking.
predicates.respondent_used_available_legal_remedy: The alleged contemnor pursued a legal remedy available to address the dispute.
predicates.remedy_addressed_company_management_dead: The legal proceeding concerned a deadlock affecting the management or operation of a company.
predicates.interim_facilitator_arrangement_recogniz: A forum made interim directions appointing or empowering a facilitator, and the court whose order is said to have been breached acknowledged that arrangement or allowed it to continue.
predicates.interim_orders_not_set_aside: The interim directions relied on in the dispute had not been set aside when the alleged conduct occurred.
predicates.wilful_disobedience: The alleged contemnor deliberately and intentionally failed to obey a court order or breached an undertaking given to a court.

issues.definition: When a civil-contempt proceeding concerns a respondent’s use of an available legal remedy to address a company-management deadlock, and the related interim arrangement remains in force without proof of wilful disobedience, contempt is not established.

issues.legal_issue: An interim order remains operative and must be obeyed while an objection to the issuing forum’s jurisdiction is undecided, unless the order is set aside or modified.
material_facts: The petitioner objected to the company-law forum’s jurisdiction and maintainability but did not obtain an order setting aside its interim directions.
The forum had made interim directions regulating company affairs while the proceedings remained pending.
The Supreme Court did not decide whether the company-law proceedings were ultimately maintainable and left the parties free to raise jurisdictional objections in those proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The jurisdictional objection did not itself invalidate the interim directions; they remained binding while in force, without the Court deciding the ultimate maintainability of the proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: In Tayabbhai M. Bagasarwalla v. Hind Rubber Industries (P) Ltd., the Court held that an objection to jurisdiction does not immediately disable a forum from making interim orders. Such orders operate until the forum decides that it lacks jurisdiction, though they may then be modified or brought to an end. While in force, they must be obeyed, and a breach committed before the jurisdictional decision may be punished. The Court also noted that the relevant interim powers arose under Sections 397, 398, and 403 of the Companies Act, 1956, but expressly left the ultimate maintainability of the pending proceedings open.

rule.if: pending_interim_order_proceeding and interim_order_made and jurisdiction_objection_undecided and order_not_set_aside_or_modified

predicates.pending_interim_order_proceeding: A proceeding is pending in which a forum has made an interim order while its authority to hear the matter is disputed.
predicates.interim_order_made: The forum has issued an interim order regulating the parties’ conduct or the affairs in dispute.
predicates.jurisdiction_objection_undecided: The objection to the forum’s jurisdiction has not yet been determined.
predicates.order_not_set_aside_or_modified: No competent order has set aside or modified the interim order.

issues.definition: If a forum has made an interim order in a pending proceeding and its jurisdiction is still under challenge, the order remains binding unless it has been set aside or modified.

issues.legal_issue: A request in a contempt proceeding to compel compliance with a facilitator’s decision need not be granted when the contempt petition is dismissed and a statutory forum is available to seek relief.
material_facts: The respondents applied for directions requiring the petitioner to comply with a facilitator’s decision concerning the company’s affairs.
The Court dismissed the contempt petition and declined to express a view on the merits of the application for directions.
The proceedings formerly pending before the company-law forum had transferred to the National Company Law Tribunal after the insolvency legislation came into force.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to issue the requested directions under Article 142 and disposed of the application by leaving the parties to pursue the available statutory remedy before the National Company Law Tribunal.
issues.legal_principle: The Court found that the circumstances did not warrant directions under Article 142 of the Constitution. It left the parties to pursue the statutory remedy available before the National Company Law Tribunal and expressed no opinion on the merits of the application.

predicates.direction_application_in_contempt_procee: A party seeks directions in a contempt proceeding requiring another party to comply with a facilitator’s decision.
predicates.underlying_contempt_petition_dismissed: The court dismisses the contempt petition in which the directions are sought.
predicates.statutory_forum_available: A statutory forum is available to consider the requested relief.

issues.definition: When a directions application is made in a contempt proceeding, the contempt petition is dismissed, and a statutory forum is available, the court may decline the directions and leave the parties to that statutory remedy.
